explanations.explanation: True, baker. The letter says, “On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets.” (Hebrews 1:1) Many times, many ways, and the prophets carried the words. That's the opening act before the big turn in the next verse.

Careful, friend, because the text says the opposite. “…God spoke to our fathers through the prophets.” (Hebrews 1:1) It happened on many past occasions and in many different ways. So the prophets really were the ones through whom God spoke.

His Son. The letter says, “But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son…” (Hebrews 1:2) After all those prophets, God speaks by the Son Himself. I think that's the turn the whole opening hangs on.

Judges are a fair guess, since the book of Judges tells how God raised up judges for His people (Judges 2:16). But this verse names someone else. It says, “…He has spoken to us by His Son…” (Hebrews 1:2). The answer is the Son.
Scribes are not mentioned anywhere in these verses, friend. The text says God “…has spoken to us by His Son…” (Hebrews 1:2). That's who the verse names.
Heir. The verse says God appointed His Son “…heir of all things…” (Hebrews 1:2) All things, baker. I've got one bakery and one cookie planet, so "all things" is a little over my head.

A steward looks after what belongs to somebody else, so it's a fair guess. But the verse says God appointed Him “…heir of all things…” (Hebrews 1:2). Heir is the word the text gives, so that's the word we keep.

A witness tells what happened, and that sounds close, but it isn't the word here. The verse says God appointed Him “…heir of all things…” (Hebrews 1:2). The same verse says the universe was made through Him. That's a lot more than standing by and watching.

True. The verse says God appointed Him heir, “…and through whom He made the universe.” (Hebrews 1:2) So the Son is heir of all things and the one the universe was made through. That's a long way from my little planet and my ovens.
That one is right there in the verse, friend. “…and through whom He made the universe.” (Hebrews 1:2) So the text says God made it through the Son. Sometimes the plain answer is the true one.
All things. The letter says the Son is “…upholding all things by His powerful word.” (Hebrews 1:3) Not one thing, not a few, all of it. I can barely keep my own hat from sliding on a windy day.
Temple walls are a solid guess, but they aren't in this passage. The verse says the Son is “…upholding all things by His powerful word.” (Hebrews 1:3) Walls are just a small slice of all things.

Jerusalem is a big city, but the verse goes way bigger than that. The Son is “…upholding all things by His powerful word.” (Hebrews 1:3) A whole city is still just a piece of all things. Can't get bigger than all, baker.

explanations.answer: Sat down at the right hand of the Majesty
explanations.explanation: He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty. The verse says, “After He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.” (Hebrews 1:3) The order matters, baker: purification first, then the sitting. I think that's a verse worth reading slowly.

explanations.answer: Stood guard at the gates of heaven
explanations.explanation: Standing guard at the gates isn't in this verse. It says, “After He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.” (Hebrews 1:3) Sat down, not stood. It's a different picture from the one in your answer.

explanations.answer: Went back to speaking through the prophets
explanations.explanation: Speaking through the prophets is the past in this letter. Verse 2 says that in these last days God has spoken by His Son. Then verse 3 says that after the purification for sins, “…He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.” No going back to the old way is mentioned.

Not quite, friend. The text says, “So He became as far superior to the angels as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs.” (Hebrews 1:4) Superior, not equal. The writer sets the Son above the angels, and the verses after this back it up.

Right, He isn't on their level. “So He became as far superior to the angels as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs.” (Hebrews 1:4) The name He inherited is more excellent than theirs. The writer goes on to back that up with what God said.
“You are My Son…” The writer asks which of the angels God ever told that line (Hebrews 1:5). It's asked as a question, and no angel is named as the one it was said to. Those words belong to the Son.

Priest is a fair guess, but it isn't in this verse. The writer asks which of the angels God ever told, “You are My Son…” (Hebrews 1:5). The words are about a Son and a Father. That's the line no angel is shown hearing.

Prophets came up in verse 1, so this one is tempting. But the writer asks which of the angels God ever told, “You are My Son…” (Hebrews 1:5). The word is Son, not prophet. The writer is making a point about the Son here.
Worship Him. When God brings His firstborn into the world, He says, “Let all God’s angels worship Him.” (Hebrews 1:6) ALL of them, friend. Not just a few.
Guarding a throne sounds like angel work, but that isn't what the verse says. God says, “Let all God’s angels worship Him.” (Hebrews 1:6) The word is worship. The firstborn gets worshiped.
Leading armies sounds mighty, but it's not in this verse. What God says is, “Let all God’s angels worship Him.” (Hebrews 1:6) Worship, from all of them. No armies mentioned.

Servants. The verse says, “He makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire.” (Hebrews 1:7) The writer sets that next to what God says about the Son. And at the end of the chapter he calls the angels ministering spirits sent to serve.

Sons is the word the writer saved for somebody else. The verse says, “He makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire.” (Hebrews 1:7) Back in verse 5, the words “You are My Son…” are the ones no angel is shown hearing.

Kings would be a big title, and this verse doesn't give it. It says, “He makes His angels winds, His servants flames of fire.” (Hebrews 1:7) The throne talk comes in the very next verse, and it's about the Son.
True. God says about the Son, “Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever, and justice is the scepter of Your kingdom.” (Hebrews 1:8) Forever and ever, baker. No end to that throne in the text.
The text says the opposite, friend. God says about the Son, “Your throne, O God, endures forever and ever…” (Hebrews 1:8) It doesn't wear out and it doesn't end. Forever and ever is the whole phrase.

explanations.answer: Anointed Him with the oil of joy
explanations.explanation: Anointed Him with the oil of joy. The verse says, “therefore God, Your God, has anointed You above Your companions with the oil of joy.” (Hebrews 1:9) The word “therefore” ties it to the Son loving righteousness and hating wickedness. Above His companions, too.

explanations.answer: Clothed Him in a robe of gold
explanations.explanation: A robe of gold is a fun picture, but it isn't in this verse. God “…has anointed You above Your companions with the oil of joy.” (Hebrews 1:9) The oil of joy is what the text gives. Gold isn't mentioned here at all.

explanations.answer: Gave Him a seat among the angels
explanations.explanation: Among the angels isn't what the verse says. It says God “…has anointed You above Your companions with the oil of joy.” (Hebrews 1:9) The oil of joy is what the text gives. And in verse 13 the writer asks which of the angels God ever told to sit at His right hand.

Not quite, friend. The line says, “In the beginning, O Lord, You laid the foundations of the earth, and the heavens are the work of Your hands.” (Hebrews 1:10) It says Your hands, the Lord's, and never mentions the angels' hands. The heavens are His work.
False, and good catch. The line says, “…the heavens are the work of Your hands.” (Hebrews 1:10) That's the Lord's hands, not the angels'. The same line has Him laying the foundations of the earth.

He remains the same. The line says, “They will perish, but You remain…” (Hebrews 1:11) and then, “but You remain the same, and Your years will never end.” (Hebrews 1:12) The heavens change like a garment, and He doesn't.

Growing old is what the heavens do, not what the line says about Him. They “…will all wear out like a garment.” (Hebrews 1:11) But “…You remain the same, and Your years will never end.” (Hebrews 1:12) No growing old for Him.

That's close, but it lands on the other side of the word “but.” The line says the heavens will be changed like a garment, “but You remain the same…” (Hebrews 1:12) The change belongs to them. The Son stays the same.

Enemies. God says, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet…” (Hebrews 1:13) The writer asks which of the angels was ever told that. Sit at My right hand is not an angel's line in this passage.

Children isn't the word in this line. God says, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet…” (Hebrews 1:13) A footstool for the Son's feet is made of enemies. That's the word the text gives.

Brothers is a gentle guess, but this line has no brothers in it. God says, “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet…” (Hebrews 1:13) The word is enemies. Easy to mix up when you're thinking family.

Those who will inherit salvation. The writer asks, “Are not the angels ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14) So the angels are sent to serve them. That's the angels' job description in this verse.

explanations.answer: The kings of the whole earth
explanations.explanation: Kings are not in this verse, friend. The writer asks, “Are not the angels ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14) The ones served are those who will inherit salvation. No crowns mentioned.

explanations.answer: The priests serving in the temple
explanations.explanation: Priests are not named in this verse. It says the angels are “…ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1:14) Those who will inherit salvation are the ones served. A temple isn't mentioned.

True. The verse says, “We must pay closer attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away.” (Hebrews 2:1) Closer attention, so we do not drift away. That “so that” tells us why the attention matters.

The writer really does say it, friend. “We must pay closer attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away.” (Hebrews 2:1) Closer attention is the way to avoid drifting. The word “therefore” ties it to everything said about the Son.

Binding. The verse says, “For if the message spoken by angels was binding, and every transgression and disobedience received its just punishment…” (Hebrews 2:2) The “if” sets up the big question in the next verse. A binding message is one that holds.

Optional is what plenty of people tell their snooze button. But the verse says, “…the message spoken by angels was binding…” (Hebrews 2:2). Binding is the opposite of optional. The same verse says every transgression and disobedience received its just punishment.

Forgotten isn't the word, friend. The verse says, “…the message spoken by angels was binding…” (Hebrews 2:2). It also says every transgression and disobedience received its just punishment. Binding is the word the text gives.
Not quite, friend. The writer asks, “…how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?” (Hebrews 2:3) He doesn't point to any way out. The question is the warning.
Right. The writer asks, “…how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?” (Hebrews 2:3) He doesn't offer any way out for neglect. That's why he said earlier to pay closer attention.

Those who heard Him. The verse says this salvation “…was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard Him…” (Hebrews 2:3) So the Lord announced it first, and those who heard Him confirmed it to us. The writer includes himself in that “us.”

Angels do appear in this passage, but not here. The message spoken by angels is in verse 2. This salvation “…was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard Him…” (Hebrews 2:3). The confirming came from those who heard Him.

The prophets show up in verse 1 of this letter, so it's a natural pick. But this verse says the salvation “…was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard Him…” (Hebrews 2:3). Those who heard Him are the ones who confirmed it.

explanations.answer: Through signs and wonders and miracles
explanations.explanation: Signs and wonders and miracles. The verse says it was “…affirmed by God through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit…” (Hebrews 2:4) That's God's own affirming. The gifts of the Holy Spirit are named right alongside the signs.

explanations.answer: Through a new temple and new laws
explanations.explanation: A new temple and new laws aren't in this verse. It says the salvation was “…affirmed by God through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit…” (Hebrews 2:4). That's the list the text gives. Nothing about building anything.

explanations.answer: Through angels speaking from the clouds
explanations.explanation: Angels speaking from the clouds isn't in the verse. It says God affirmed it “…through signs, wonders, various miracles, and gifts of the Holy Spirit…” (Hebrews 2:4). Angels came up in verse 2, but they aren't part of this list.
True. The verse says God affirmed it with “…gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to His will.” (Hebrews 2:4) According to His will, baker. The gifts are handed out the way He chooses.

The verse says it plainly, friend. “…gifts of the Holy Spirit distributed according to His will.” (Hebrews 2:4) So the writer does say it, and that makes this one True. In my bakery I'd hand out every topping to everybody, but the text says these gifts are distributed according to His will.
